title: Infra GPU Capacity, Cloud Networking, IaC & CI/CD Playbook
author: Maya Patel
content:
Overview:
This playbook consolidates Redwood Inference's operational standards and runbooks for GPU fleet capacity, cloud accounts & networking, Terraform/IaC modules, and CI/CD pipelines that build and deploy infra artifacts. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners responsible for sustaining predictable inference capacity and secure networking across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Scope:
- GPU fleet sizing and autoscaling policies
- Cloud account structure and networking baseline (VPCs, subnets, peering, egress)
- Terraform module conventions, state management, and CI pipeline rules
- CI/CD steps for infra changes, builds, and rollout to staging/production
- Runbooks for common capacity/networking incidents and upgrade checklists

Goals and SLOs:
- Maintain average GPU utilization target: 55%–70% during business hours with 20–30% headroom for traffic spikes.
- P95 request queue latency < 200ms; P99 queue latency < 1s for routing and batching services.
- Incident MTTR targets: 30 minutes for degraded scheduling; 4 hours for complex capacity replenishment.

Owners and Signals:
- Primary owner: eng-infra (infra@g.redwood)
- Secondary/integrations: eng-sre (sre@g.redwood), eng-serving-runtime (runtime@g.redwood)
- Key metrics (telemetry):
  - gpu.pool.utilization.avg (1m/5m)
  - gpu.node.free_count
  - scheduler.queue_length, scheduler.p99_latency
  - instance.preemptions, spot.interruption_rate
  - terraform.run.plan_failures, ci.pipeline.duration

GPU Fleet Capacity Planning (methodology):
1. Baseline demand: aggregate historical token throughput and average model memory per request. Use 6–12 week window to smooth seasonality.
2. Working set sizing: compute per-model memory and peak concurrency to derive minimum GPUs required. Example formula:
   - required_gpus = ceil((peak_concurrent_memory + system_overhead) / gpu_memory_per_node)
3. Utilization target: size fleet to target 60% utilization under steady-state. Reserve an additional 20% capacity for burst tolerance and preemption.
4. Forecast cadence: weekly short-term forecast (1–2 weeks) and monthly capacity planning for procurement. Maintain a 30–60 day lead time for dedicated capacity purchases.

Autoscaling & Scheduling Policies:
- Horizontal autoscaling (preferred): add/remove worker instances in the GPU node pool using Capacity Manager service.
- Scale-up triggers:
  1. scheduler.queue_length > 50 for 60s OR
  2. gpu.pool.utilization.avg > 75% for 90s
- Scale-down policy: only when sustained utilization < 45% for 10m and free GPU count > min_reserve.
- Spot/Preemptible instances: allow up to 30% of pool but always maintain a minimum of 2 reserved on-demand nodes per region.

Networking and Cloud Accounts:
- Org hierarchy: separate accounts/projects per environment (prod/staging/dev) and per tenant where required (private deployments).
- VPC design:
  - Per-region VPCs with standardized subnet naming: public, app, gpu, management.
  - Strict egress via NATs and centralized egress endpoints for compliance logging.
  - Transit/Peering: use shared transit hub for cross-account routing; avoid complex mesh peering.
- Firewall/security groups:
  - GPU nodes accept inbound from internal app subnets on specific ports (gRPC 7000–7010, SSH only via bastion).
  - Management network limited to engops CIDR + jump hosts; all access logged to audit log.
- Private deployments: provide documented bootstrap scripts for customer VPC onboarding; require VPN or Direct Connect with encryption in transit.

Terraform / IaC Module Standards:
- Repository layout: modules/ (reusable), environments/ (prod/staging/dev composed of root modules), examples/.
- Module contracts: each module must include: README.md, inputs.tf (documented), outputs.tf, tests/ (unit/terratest or kitchen-terraform).
- State management: remote state in encrypted backend (S3/GCS) + DynamoDB/lock table. Use one state per logical environment and avoid monolithic global state.
- Naming and tagging: all resources must include tags: service, team, environment, cost_center, owner.
- Linting & validation: tflint, terraform validate, checkov for security scanning.
- Secret handling: no secrets in repo. Use KMS/Secret Manager referenced by data sources at runtime.
- Example workflow snippet:
  - terraform init -backend-config=env/${ENV}.backend
  - terraform plan -var-file=env/${ENV}.tfvars
  - terraform apply after merge and approval

CI/CD and Build Pipelines (infra):
- Branching: trunk-based for infra with short-lived feature branches.
- PR requirements:
  1. Passing unit tests and linters (tflint, fmt)
  2. Successful terraform plan in pipeline (artifact stored)
  3. Reviewer approval from infra or owning service
- Pipeline stages for environment changes:
  1. Lint & static analysis
  2. Unit tests and module tests
  3. Plan (create plan artifact and upload)
  4. Manual approval gate for prod (with list of approvers)
  5. Apply (run in a short-lived runner with least privilege)
- Canary deployment model for infra: roll out changes to staging, then to a small subset of GPU nodes in prod (10%) for at least 30 minutes while monitoring key metrics before full rollout.
- Immutable artifacts: build container images for infra sidecars (monitoring, exporters) with sha-based tags.

Runbooks (operational procedures):
1. High scheduler queue / latency (Immediate):
   - Pager to oncall (infra capacity).
   - Check metrics: scheduler.queue_length, gpu.pool.utilization.avg, gpu.node.free_count.
   - If utilization sustained >85%: scale up by 20% (follow autoscaler api: curl -X POST https://capacity-manager/api/v1/scale -d '{"pool":"gpu-pool-01","delta":20}').
   - If scale fails or spot preemption high: trigger fallback traffic routing to lower-cost/latency model variants (see routing policy).
   - Post-incident: open ticket, record root cause, update forecast.
2. Single GPU node OOM or crash:
   - Remove node from pool: gcloud compute instances set-labels NODE --labels=maintenance=true (or equivalent awscli).
   - Drain workloads and cordon node: kubectl drain NODE --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data.
   - Collect logs: /var/log/gpu-monitor.log, dmesg, nvidia-smi -q > /tmp/nvidia-smi.txt.
   - Recreate node from IaC if hardware fault: terraform taint module.gpu_node[...] && terraform apply.
3. Unexpected spot preemptions / capacity loss:
   - Reduce reliance on spot for critical pools; increase on-demand minimum.
   - If customer impact: enable emergency routing rule to route traffic to dedicated capacity region.

Upgrade and Rollout Checklist (before IaC or kernel changes):
- Verify staging cluster passing all perf and regression tests (throughput and latency).
- Take snapshot/AMI of a golden node; ensure automated rollback image exists.
- Notify downstream teams and open maintenance window if >10% expected capacity change.
- Run terraform plan and store plan artifact; require two approvers for prod.
- Canary: apply to 10% nodes, monitor for 30–60 minutes, then continue rollout.

Diagnostics and Useful Commands:
- Terraform plan against prod: 
  terraform init -backend-config=env/prod.backend && terraform plan -var-file=env/prod.tfvars -out=prod.plan
- Inspect GPU metrics (promql): 
  sum by(pool) (rate(gpu_utilization_seconds_total[5m])) / count by(pool) (gpu_total_seconds)
- Drain node: kubectl drain NODE --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data
- Force scale via capacity-manager: curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' https://capacity-manager.internal/api/scale -d '{"pool":"gpu-pool-01","count":+4}'

Post-incident & Continuous Improvement:
- For every capacity incident create an incident card and attach: timeline, root cause, mitigation, and follow-ups.
- Maintain a capacity runbook index and link to retrospective action items.
- Quarterly capacity review with SRE, serving runtime, and product to adjust forecasting assumptions and procurement.
